providers.name: AWS RDS for PostgreSQL

branching.mechanism: No branching. Restore a DB snapshot or do a point-in-time restore, which always creates a new DB instance. Snapshot restores lazy-load blocks from S3; PITR initializes new volumes at up to 4 TiB/hour on gp3/io2.
branching.freeTier: No branching feature on any tier. Restores are ordinary new instances (AWS Free Tier eligibility for restored instances not verified).
branching.cost: Billed as a full new DB instance (compute plus storage) for as long as it runs.

sources.quote: You can't restore from a DB snapshot to an existing DB instance; you create a new DB instance when you restore the snapshot.
The DB instance continues to load data in the background. This is known as lazy loading.
If you access data that hasn't been loaded yet, the DB instance immediately downloads the requested data from Amazon S3, and then continues loading the rest of the data in the background.
You can restore a DB instance to a specific point in time, creating a new DB instance without modifying the source DB instance.
volumes continue to load data blocks from Amazon S3 in the background at a rate of up to 4 TiB per hour for volumes that use gp3 or io2 Block Express storage.

majorUpgrade.method: Self-service in-place upgrade (pg_upgrade) via ModifyDBInstance, or RDS Blue/Green Deployments (green copy kept in sync, then switchover). Blue/Green uses logical replication for major upgrades in some cases, so DDL, DCL, sequences and new large objects are not replicated.
majorUpgrade.downtimeClaim: In-place: downtime not quantified; in-Region read replicas are upgraded with the primary and 'might increase downtime'. Blue/Green: 'switchover typically takes under a minute'.
majorUpgrade.statistics: Docs say optimizer statistics are not transferred; run ANALYZE on every database after the upgrade.
majorUpgrade.rollback: No in-place rollback. With backup retention > 0, RDS takes snapshots before and after the upgrade; roll back by restoring the pre-upgrade snapshot to a new instance. Blue/Green keeps the old blue instance after switchover (it keeps billing).
majorUpgrade.latestMajor: 18 (18.6 is the newest upgrade target listed). PostgreSQL 19 RC1 only in the RDS Database Preview environment.

sources.quote: doesn't apply major version upgrades automatically. To perform a major version upgrade, you modify your database manually.
read replica upgrades might increase downtime on the primary DB instance.
If your backup retention period is greater than 0, the upgrade process creates DB snapshots of your database before and after upgrading.
Optimizer statistics aren't transferred during a major version upgrade, so you need to regenerate all statistics to avoid performance issues.
The switchover typically takes under a minute with no data loss and no need for application changes.
Under certain conditions, RDS for PostgreSQL uses logical replication instead of physical replication to keep the green environment in sync with the blue environment.
Data definition language (DDL) statements, such as CREATE TABLE and CREATE SCHEMA, aren't replicated from the blue environment to the green environment.
You must delete the blue/green deployment and all green databases, then recreate it.
A retained blue DB instance still incurs charges for compute and storage until you delete

providers.name: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL

branching.mechanism: Aurora fast database cloning: copy-on-write clone of the cluster volume into a new, independent cluster. Up to 15 copy-on-write clones per source; the 16th is a full copy (acts like PITR). Same Region only; cross-account cloning via AWS RAM.
branching.cost: Clone is a new cluster: you pay for its DB instances. Storage is shared; the clone pays only for pages it changes (source keeps paying for shared pages).

sources.quote: Aurora uses a copy-on-write protocol to create a clone.
Creating a clone is faster and more space-efficient than physically copying the data using

You can create up to 15 clones that use the copy-on-write protocol from each source Aurora DB cluster. After a source DB cluster has 15 copy-on-write clones, the next clone that you create from that DB cluster is a full copy.
You can't create a clone in a different AWS Region from the source Aurora DB cluster.
For pages that are identical between the source volume and the clone, the storage charges apply only to the original cluster.

majorUpgrade.method: Self-service in-place major upgrade (Aurora snapshots the cluster first), or Aurora Blue/Green Deployments.
majorUpgrade.downtimeClaim: In-place: not quantified. Blue/Green: 'typically under a minute depending on your workload'.
majorUpgrade.statistics: Optimizer statistics are not carried over; run ANALYZE on every database.
majorUpgrade.rollback: Restore the automatic 'preupgrade' cluster snapshot to get the old version back (new cluster). PITR is blocked during the upgrade.
majorUpgrade.latestMajor: 18 (Aurora PostgreSQL 18.6 released 29 Sep 2026). Aurora adopts new majors within 8 months of the community .1 release.

providers.name: Xata

branching.mechanism: Copy-on-write storage snapshot: a child branch has the parent's exact schema and data at creation; it then runs as an independent Postgres instance in the same region. No merge, no reset in place.
branching.freeTier: No free tier (free trial only; open-source core is free to self-host).
branching.cost: Each running branch is billed hourly by instance type (scale-to-zero makes idle branches $0 compute); unchanged storage is shared. Xata Cloud from $0.012/hr + $0.28/GB/mo. Branch count limits depend on plan.

sources.quote: a child branch contains the exact schema and data of its parent at the moment of creation, regardless of database size.
Creating a child branch copies the parent's schema and data using a Copy-on-Write storage snapshot, so it completes in seconds even for terabyte-scale databases.
Each running branch has its own compute instance, billed hourly by instance type.
The number of branches per project and the branch creation rate depend on your plan.
